definition: ELKI (Environment for Developing KDD-Applications Supported by Index-Structures) is a data mining (KDD, knowledge discovery in databases) software framework developed for use in research and teaching.
details: It was originally created by the database systems research unit at LMU Munich, Germany, led by Professor Hans-Peter Kriegel. The project has continued at the Technical University of Dortmund, Germany. It aims at allowing the development and evaluation of advanced data mining algorithms and their interaction with database index structures.

explainer.lead: ELKI is a software framework for building and testing data-mining methods, especially where database index structures can support their work. It gives researchers and students a common setting for developing algorithms and evaluating how they behave.

tiers.eli5: Imagine trying different ways to sort a big box of toys, with special shelves that help you find toys faster. ELKI is like a workbench where researchers and students can build those sorting methods and test how well they work with the shelves. It helps them compare ideas instead of starting from scratch every time.
tiers.practitioner: Use ELKI as a research and teaching framework when developing or evaluating data-mining algorithms, particularly experiments involving database index structures. A typical workflow is to implement or select an algorithm, run it on data, and evaluate its behavior with the relevant index support. Keep the experimental question clear: an algorithm’s performance and its interaction with an index structure are related but distinct concerns.
tiers.paperLevel: ELKI is a KDD software framework for developing and evaluating advanced data-mining algorithms A and their interaction with database index structures I, supporting comparative study of algorithmic behavior under different indexing choices. It was originally created by the database systems research unit at LMU Munich, led by Professor Hans-Peter Kriegel, and the project later continued at the Technical University of Dortmund. It is a framework rather than a formal model or a single algorithm, so it has no defining objective function.

explainer.example: A student testing a clustering algorithm on a collection of two-dimensional points can implement and evaluate it in ELKI, then repeat the experiment with support from a database index structure. Comparing the runs helps the student study not only the clustering method but also how its interaction with indexing changes its behavior.

explainer.intuition: Testing a data-mining algorithm fairly requires more than the algorithm itself: data access and indexing can also shape the experiment. ELKI brings algorithm development, database index structures, and evaluation into one research-oriented framework.
howItWorks: Choose or develop a data-mining algorithm within the framework.
Provide the data needed for the experiment.
Use relevant database index structures to support data access.
Run the algorithm and evaluate its behavior.
Compare algorithms or indexing choices to understand their interaction.
explainer.whyItMatters: ELKI supports repeatable development and evaluation in research and teaching while making data access part of the experimental picture. That matters because studying an algorithm together with database index structures can reveal effects that an algorithm-only view would miss.
misconceptions: ELKI is a framework, not a single clustering or classification algorithm.
It is not only a finished end-user application; algorithm development and evaluation are central aims.
Its interest in index structures does not mean indexing is the only subject being evaluated.
